questions.q: Per this lesson, what question does a data dictionary answer, as distinct from a glossary?
options: What is this specific table or column, structurally?
What does this concept mean to the business?
Who is accountable for the overall governance program?
How much does this data cost to store?
questions.explain: The glossary answers meaning; the dictionary answers physical, structural facts about a specific table or column.

questions.q: Why is a data dictionary organized around tables and columns, when Lesson 6 warned against organizing a glossary that way?
options: Because a dictionary is documenting physical structures directly, which is exactly what it's for
Because Lesson 6's warning was a mistake that this lesson corrects
Because dictionaries and glossaries are actually the same artifact with different names
Because tables are easier to alphabetize than business concepts
questions.explain: A glossary organized around tables restates the schema instead of capturing business meaning; a dictionary organized around tables is doing precisely its intended job.

questions.q: Which of these is a field a dictionary entry needs that a glossary entry does NOT typically carry, per this lesson?
options: Data type and nullability
A name
An owner
A status (approved, draft, deprecated)
questions.explain: Both share the six core metadata fields from Lesson 3, but structural facts like data type, nullability, and constraints are specific to the dictionary's job of describing physical objects.

questions.q: Can a single business glossary term map to more than one data dictionary entry, per this lesson?
options: Yes — a concept like 'Active Customer' can link to multiple columns across tables that help calculate it
No — every glossary term maps to exactly one column, always
No — glossary terms and dictionary entries are never linked to each other
Only glossary terms with fewer than five letters can have multiple links
questions.explain: A glossary term describes a business concept that can be implemented by several physical columns; the dictionary and glossary link together rather than being a strict one-to-one mapping.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does a well-built metadata program do with glossary terms and dictionary entries?
options: Links them together so someone can navigate from a business definition to its implementation, or the reverse
Keeps them in completely separate, unconnected systems with no cross-reference
Merges them into a single artifact with no distinction between business and technical metadata
Deletes the dictionary once the glossary is complete
questions.explain: The two-way link lets someone start from either the business definition or a specific column and navigate to the other — Chapter 5's data catalogs are largely built around making this link easy to use.
